ledger.sentence: Loperamide is a medicine for diarrhoea that slows the activity of the bowel so that stools firm up.
It can help with short-term diarrhoea and, in adults with a doctor's diagnosis, irritable bowel syndrome, and it is not suitable for everyone.
Taking more than recommended can cause serious heart problems, and the NHS says a fast, irregular or pounding heartbeat needs urgent help.
Treating short-term diarrhoea.
ledger.note: NHS: can help with short-term diarrhoea

ledger.sentence: Helping with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in adults whose doctor has diagnosed it.
Treating longer-lasting diarrhoea from conditions such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, on prescription.
The NHS says loperamide works by slowing the activity of the bowel.
Bowel contents then move more slowly and stay in the intestine for longer, which lets more water be absorbed back into the body and firms up stools.
The US FDA describes loperamide as acting on opioid receptors in the gut to slow movement through the intestine.
The NHS says loperamide usually starts to make diarrhoea better within 1 hour.
The NHS lists headache, dizziness, constipation, feeling sick and wind as common side effects.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says loperamide can cause dizziness, tiredness and drowsiness, and that drinking alcohol makes these more likely.
The NHS advises against driving or using machinery if affected.
The NHS says signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face, lips or throat or difficulty breathing, need urgent help, and that a 999 call is the route for an emergency.

ledger.sentence: MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount of loperamide can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal.
The NHS lists a fast, irregular or pounding heartbeat, bloody stools, severe stomach pain or swelling, and fever as signs to get medical help.
The US FDA says that at much higher than recommended amounts loperamide can cause severe heart rhythm problems and death.
Over the counter, the NHS says loperamide is for anyone aged 12 or over with short-term diarrhoea, and for adults with IBS only if a doctor has diagnosed it.
Children aged 11 or under and adults with long-lasting diarrhoea need a prescription, according to the NHS.

The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis or another inflammatory bowel condition, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature among the situations where it is not suitable.
The NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough evidence about it, and that anyone pregnant should speak to a doctor first.
The NHS says breastfeeding is considered acceptable because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk and no side effects are expected in the baby.
The NHS says some medicines can affect how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil, desmopressin and other anti-diarrhoea or bowel medicines.
The NHS says loperamide can be taken alongside paracetamol or ibuprofen and does not stop contraceptive pills working, although severe diarrhoea can make the pill less reliable.
Loperamide for long-lasting diarrhoea or bowel conditions is supervised by a doctor.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says loperamide can be bought from pharmacies and shops for people aged 12 or over with short-term diarrhoea.
It is available on prescription for children aged 11 or under and for adults with long-lasting diarrhoea.
The NHS describes loperamide as a medicine to treat diarrhoea.
It can help with short-term diarrhoea and with irritable bowel syndrome that a doctor has diagnosed in an adult.
For longer-lasting diarrhoea, such as that from Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, it is available on prescription.
Loperamide slows the activity of the bowel, so the contents move more slowly and stay in the intestine for longer.
More water is then absorbed back into the body and stools become firmer.
The NHS says it usually starts to improve diarrhoea within 1 hour.
Common side effects listed by the NHS are headache, dizziness, constipation, feeling sick and wind.
Dizziness, tiredness and drowsiness are more likely with alcohol.
A fast, irregular or pounding heartbeat can be a sign of heart problems from taking too much.
Swelling of the face, lips or throat, or difficulty breathing, is an emergency: call 999.
